exam: A 45‑year‑old farmer presents with a rough, scaly plaque on his forearm; what is the most likely diagnosis and next step? — Actinic keratosis; perform dermatoscopy or biopsy if suspicious, then treat with cryotherapy.

A patient with HIV develops multiple painful erythematous patches after a beach trip; how does immunosuppression alter management? — Higher risk of progression; treat sunburn aggressively and monitor for early SCC, consider biopsy of persistent lesions.
You see a patient with a blistering sunburn covering >30 % of body surface; what immediate care is required? — Fluid resuscitation, analgesia, wound care; treat as a burn, watch for infection.
Which UV wavelength causes the majority of DNA pyrimidine dimers? — UV‑B (280‑320 nm).
A lesion on the ear is pearly with telangiectasia; what distinguishes it from actinic keratosis? — Presence of central ulceration and rolled borders suggests basal cell carcinoma; biopsy confirms.
Why is topical 5‑fluorouracil preferred over systemic chemotherapy for widespread actinic keratoses in a low‑resource setting? — It is inexpensive, locally applied, and avoids systemic toxicity.
A patient reports taking doxycycline and now has a severe rash after sun exposure; what is the mechanism? — Drug‑induced photosensitivity (photo‑allergic reaction) amplifies UV damage.
What red‑flag symptom in a patient with chronic sun‑damaged skin warrants urgent referral? — Rapid change in size, ulceration, or bleeding of a lesion.
ai.title: Sunlight Exposure and Skin Pathology
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Excess ultraviolet (UV) radiation damages skin DNA, leading to acute photodermatitis and chronic conditions such as actinic keratosis and skin cancer. In low‑resource settings, diagnosis relies on clinical clues and limited investigations.

b: Acute UV‑induced erythema (sunburn) appears 2‑24 h after exposure.
Actinic keratosis: rough, scaly papules on chronically exposed sites.
Skin cancer suspicion: new, changing, or non‑healing lesions.
sections.p: Sunlight exposure refers to the amount of ultraviolet (UV) radiation reaching the skin. Pathologic effects range from acute erythema to premalignant lesions and malignancy.

b: Sunburn: 1st‑degree (erythema only), 2nd‑degree (partial thickness blistering), 3rd‑degree (full‑thickness necrosis).
Actinic keratosis: isolated vs. field‑cancerized skin.
Skin cancer: in‑situ (Bowen disease) vs. invasive (depth of invasion).
sections.p: Severity is graded by clinical appearance and depth of skin injury.

b: UV‑B (280‑320 nm) – main driver of DNA pyrimidine dimers.
UV‑A (320‑400 nm) – contributes to photo‑aging and deeper dermal damage.
Fair skin, chronic outdoor work, lack of protective clothing, and immunosuppression (HIV, transplant).
Photosensitising drugs (e.g., tetracyclines, sulfonamides).
sections.p: UV radiation is the primary cause; other contributors modify risk.

b: Acute: painful erythema, warmth, edema, possible blistering.
Chronic: rough, sand‑paper skin, telangiectasia, lentigines, actinic keratoses.
Malignancy: ulcerated, pearly, or pigmented lesions, often on face, ears, hands.
sections.p: Presentation varies with acute vs. chronic exposure.

t.b: Confirms diagnosis; distinguishes sunburn from infection – look for uniform erythema, absence of pus.
Evaluates lesion architecture – helps differentiate actinic keratosis from squamous cell carcinoma.
Answers: Is the lesion benign, premalignant, or malignant?
Assesses deficiency when sunlight is limited.

b: Rapidly enlarging or ulcerating lesion.
Bleeding, pain, or crusting unresponsive to simple care.
Signs of infection over sunburn (pus, fever).
Immunocompromised host with extensive lesions.
sections.p: Identify patients who need urgent referral.

b: Acute sunburn: cool compresses, oral analgesia, hydration; avoid NSAIDs if ulcer risk.
Actinic keratosis: cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen (first‑line), topical 5‑fluorouracil or imiquimod where available.
Skin cancer: surgical excision with clear margins; refer for radiotherapy/chemotherapy if needed.
Vitamin D supplementation for deficient patients (oral cholecalciferol).
sections.p: Treat the acute injury, remove premalignant lesions, and prevent future damage.

b: Re‑examine treated lesions at 4‑6 weeks.
Teach patients to use broad‑spectrum sunscreen (SPF 30+), wear hats, and seek shade.
Encourage regular self‑examination, especially in high‑risk groups.
sections.p: Regular skin checks and education are essential.

b: Contact dermatitis – localized to area of allergen, not diffuse sun‑exposed skin.
Tinea corporis – ring‑shaped lesions with central clearing, not rough sand‑paper texture.
Drug‑induced photosensitivity – occurs after drug exposure, often with a defined timeline.
sections.p: Conditions that mimic UV‑induced skin changes.

b: Dermatoscopic features of benign actinic keratosis may overlap with early SCC; biopsy is definitive.
Vitamin D levels can be normal despite inadequate sun protection if dietary intake is high.

whenToSeekHelp: Fever, increasing pain, or pus over a sunburn
Any suspicion of skin cancer in an immunocompromised patient
